summary: The Tree height calculator returns tree height. The inputs are distance from the tree, the angle between the viewpoint and the treetop and the angle between the viewpoint and the tree base. It is built for an animal, a plant or a biological process whose scale you want to put into perspective. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Tree height calculator work?
sections.html:
The Tree height calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports tree height in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the method and the tree location); then you type in the distance from the tree, the angle between the viewpoint and the treetop (β), the angle between the viewpoint and the tree base (α) and the distance from the tree (2).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Tree height calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Tree height=distance from the tree × the tangent of (angle between the viewpoint and the treetop (β)) + eye level
Eye level=distance from the tree × the tangent of (angle between the viewpoint and the tree base (α))
Tree height=distance from the tree × (-the tangent of (angle between the viewpoint and the tree base (α)) + the tangent of (angle between the viewpoint and the treetop (β)))
Length of the tree's shadow=length of your shadow × tree height ÷ your height

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Method set to Trigonometry, Tree location set to Below viewpoint, Distance from the tree = 30 m and Angle between the viewpoint and the treetop (β) = 10 deg. The calculator returns Angle between the viewpoint and the tree base (α) = 45 deg and Tree height = 35 m.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Angle between the viewpoint and the tree base (α) = 45 deg and Tree height = 35 m should be roughly the size you expected from Method set to Trigonometry and Tree location set to Below viewpoint.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Tree height calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the distance from the tree, the angle between the viewpoint and the treetop and the angle between the viewpoint and the tree base — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Tree height calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns tree height, derived from the distance from the tree, the angle between the viewpoint and the treetop and the angle between the viewpoint and the tree base. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Tree height calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the distance from the tree, the angle between the viewpoint and the treetop and the angle between the viewpoint and the tree base, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance from the tree in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance from the tree opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Angle between the viewpoint and the tree base (α) = 45 deg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Tree height calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
